## Summary

The file is a transcript of a coastal-engineering conference (opening ~28 minutes of the file are Hebrew-language introductions/music/applause with almost no usable English content, indicating this was a conference held in Israel with international speakers — this matches the later explicit mention of an Israeli reef project). Two English-language technical talks follow:

1. **~00:28:30–01:04:00** — A talk by the managing director ("Aaron"/"Aron Sailor", phonetic) of **International Coastal Management (ICM)**, a ~45-year-old Gold Coast, Australia-based coastal engineering firm working worldwide (Australia, California, Zanzibar/Tanzania, the Middle East, Europe). The talk is a general framework for "coastal resilience," using the Gold Coast as the main case study: dune systems, buried seawalls, a large-scale geotextile-tube multi-purpose artificial reef (Narrow Neck), a smaller rock reef, nearshore nourishment, and a sand bypass/backpass pumping system. A UAE project comparing an emergent breakwater vs. a submerged reef is also described, plus shorter California and Queensland examples. Audience Q&A covers sediment-transport regulation, storm/cyclone impact, and required annual sand volumes.
2. **~01:19:20–01:28:05** — A talk by a second presenter ("Will", introduced by an assistant called "Jonathan"/"John" who runs the slides) representing a company transcribed as **"Seaell"** (almost certainly a mishearing of a real mineral-accretion reef company — likely "CCell," given the described technology and its stated partnership with **Bath University** and **Imperial College**, both real UK institutions doing mineral-accretion/electro-deposition reef research). This company grows rock structures on bamboo/willow skeletons using electrical mineral accretion, has iterated through ~50 structure designs to settle on "hyperboloid" reef units, and — critically — describes their **largest reef to date, installed in Israel**, where bamboo was unavailable so willow was substituted.

For the Israel-focused HTML survey, the single most load-bearing passage in this file is the "Seaell"/CCell talk's description of an Israeli installation (no city named) using willow instead of bamboo, "with MCC support," described as their largest reef built to date at the time of the talk. Everything else in the file is comparative/background material on how a serious coastal-engineering firm designs, builds, and evaluates artificial reefs elsewhere in the world (Gold Coast, UAE, California, Queensland), including concrete cost/size/tonnage numbers for the Gold Coast's Narrow Neck geotextile reef and a clear articulation of the submerged-vs-emergent breakwater trade-off (view preservation vs. total wave-energy exclusion) that is directly relevant to Lior's Haifa proposal.

## Artificial reefs mentioned

### 1. Narrow Neck Reef, Gold Coast, Queensland, Australia
- **Year:** "almost 20 something years ago" relative to the talk (talk itself appears recent — it references a cyclone "just a few months ago" with 15 m offshore waves, the first Gold Coast cyclone of that magnitude in ~50 years; if that storm is Cyclone Alfred, March 2025, the reef dates to roughly the early-to-mid 2000s). Not stated precisely — needs web verification.
- **Location detail:** at "Narrow Neck," a specifically vulnerable stretch of the Gold Coast where the road runs close to the beach.
- **Type:** large-scale geotextile sand containers ("big geo tubes"), described as a "multi-purpose artificial reef."
- **Size (per unit):** ~20 m long, ~5–6 m wide, fills to ~2 m high, ~300 tons when full of sand.
- **Construction method:** a "split hopper barge" dredged sand off the seabed, filled the geotextile tubes inside the barge's split hopper, then used GPS to navigate to the target location and dropped the tubes on top of each other to build the structure.
- **Cost:** not stated (no dollar figures given anywhere in the transcript for this reef).
- **Financing / who paid:** not stated.
- **Purpose:** twofold by design — (1) coastal protection (reduce wave energy reaching shore, act as an underwater groin to trap part of the ~500,000 m³/year south-to-north longshore sand transport and build up a wider buffer beach on the southern/updrift side), and (2) create a surf destination. An ecological hotspot emerged as an unplanned byproduct.
- **Design vs. built:** shaped deliberately shore-*perpendicular* rather than the traditional shore-parallel breakwater orientation, specifically so waves would have "time to break" across it and be surfable — an explicit surf-focused design KPI, since "not disrupting any kind of surfing practices along the coastline was a really important KPI for this project."
- **Outcome / why:** Functioned as intended for wave reduction and sand trapping, and did become a popular surf spot and a genuine ecological hotspot — the geocontainer material has a "furry" exterior that acted "almost like a Velcro for floating microorganisms," attracting marine life. But this became "a bit of a demise": the reef attracted so many fish that it attracted too many fishermen, who crowd the reef on calm days and drop anchors that damage the geocontainers. Described explicitly as "the first of its kind of its scale," a "pilot project," "the guinea pig which we learned a whole lot of lessons from."
- **Unexpected result:** the ecological hotspot became a liability via fishing-anchor damage — a "too much of a good thing" failure mode not part of the original design intent.
- **Citations given in the talk:** none (verbal description only, illustrated with an on-screen barge photo not present in this text file).

### 2. Second-generation rock reef, Gold Coast, Queensland, Australia
- **Year:** described as a "second phase" following directly from the Narrow Neck lessons; not dated precisely.
- **Type:** rock (not geotextile).
- **Size / cost:** not stated; presenter only says rock construction is "significantly more expensive" than geotube construction but "significantly more durable and stable" — an explicit cost/durability trade-off.
- **Purpose:** more surfing-focused KPI than Narrow Neck; same underlying mechanism (take out wave energy offshore, act as an underwater groin/control structure to trap longshore sand and build an offshore sand buffer).
- **Outcome / why:** presented as a design improvement, not a failure — but the talk notes a public-safety trade-off runs the other way: on the geotube reef, when surfers fall and hit the reef ("which I've fallen off quite a few times"), the soft geocontainer surface is "not a bad place to land," implying the harder rock reef is less forgiving for surfers who fall on it. Overall the presenter frames the choice as a multi-way trade-off between coastal structure function, coastal amenity, environmental hotspot value, public safety, cost, and constructibility.
- **Citations given:** none.

### 3. UAE coastline project (two designs on the same stretch)
- **Location:** unnamed emirate/city; "one stretch of coastline in the UAE."
- **Design A (client 1):** a fully emergent breakwater — "one long stretch" designed to keep all wave energy out, so the beach behind it "doesn't move at all."
- **Design B (client 2, same coastline):** a submerged structure in front of a different client's properties, chosen because that client wanted a stable beach but also unobstructed sea views. ICM's design approach delivered, in the presenter's words, "an 8-year stable beach guarantee behind this submerged structure."
- **Cost / size / financing:** not stated.
- **Why it matters for Israel:** this is the clearest articulated precedent in the file for the core Haifa design trade-off Lior is interested in — submerged/reef structures can preserve both beach stability and horizon views, at the cost of being less totally effective at excluding wave energy than an emergent breakwater (see nearshore-nourishment/maintenance discussion below).
- **Citations given:** none.

### 4. California — short rounded "headlands" (replacing a traditional groin field)
- **Location:** unnamed California site, described as "a place in California at the moment" (an active/current ICM project as of the talk).
- **Design vs. built:** rather than traditional groins (which fully stop longshore transport), ICM used short, rounded headland structures that allow natural longshore sand transport to continue, just more slowly.
- **Related smaller project:** "a nearshore breakwater... but on a really smaller scale" was also mentioned as a California example, used to create small rather than extreme changes in the coastline.
- **Context from Q&A:** a large marina built in California "back in the 60s" created severe downdrift sediment-blocking problems; ICM is now working there to mitigate problems created ~50 years ago, since the original developer had no retroactive obligation and the marina cannot practically be removed. The suggested/likely fix is a sand backpass/pump system, though the transcript is not explicit that this has been implemented yet.
- **Cost / size / year / financing:** not stated.
- **Citations given:** none.

### 5. Queensland clay cliff project (not Gold Coast proper — described as "here in Queensland")
- **Type:** a clay-based sea cliff that was actively eroding/falling into the sea; ICM built a rock-look wall along the base to stop the erosion.
- **Design detail:** despite looking like a typical rock groin, the structure is actually built from **5-ton sandbags**, not rock — a deliberate choice because it's a popular community beach where people like to sit and walk on the structure, and sandbags are more amenable to that use than rock. Notably, ICM had to redo the job at the end of its design lifespan, and "the community actually wanted to have the sandbags instead of rocks" for the rebuild — i.e. community preference reinforced the original material choice.
- **Outcome:** implied success (no failure described), reached end of design lifespan and was refurbished in kind.
- **Cost / size / year / financing:** not stated.
- **Citations given:** none.

### 6. Unnamed breakwater/groin using geotubes for public access
- Briefly mentioned as "another example... a breakwater niche or breakwater using geo tubes rather than rocks," chosen specifically so users could walk along and access the structure — same soft-material/public-access logic as Narrow Neck.
- Location, year, cost, size: not stated.

### 7. "Seaell" (likely mis-transcribed; possibly "CCell") mineral-accretion reef trials — Bath University field trial, UK
- **Location:** field trial site described only as "about 100 meters offshore," in partnership with Bath University, UK; exact place not stated.
- **Type:** mineral-accretion ("grown rock") structures on a bamboo skeleton — a low electrical current passed through seawater raises local pH/alkalinity, causing dissolved minerals to crystallize onto the bamboo and eventually form rock "as hard as concrete," which is also described as ideal for marine-life attachment.
- **Size:** 5 units, each about 10 m long, installed ~100 m offshore.
- **Outcome:** within a couple of weeks, then confirmed about a month later, visible shoreline accretion ("broadening out") appeared in the area behind the reef, marked in red on the presenter's slide (image not present in this text file). Presenter's own summary: "with just 10 meters of reef, we've enhanced about 200 meters of shoreline," and installation itself "could install those structures in an afternoon" — framed as fast to deploy relative to impact.
- **Cost / financing / year:** not stated.
- **Citations given:** none (referred to their own lab/field data and Bath University collaboration verbally).

### 8. "Seaell" laboratory + CFD testing — Imperial College, UK
- Not a built reef but R&D: laboratory wave-basin testing of an "earlier reef design" at Imperial College, cross-validated against CFD (computational fluid dynamics) simulation, used to calculate structural pressures/loads and anchoring requirements, and to iterate designs numerically instead of relying solely on costly physical lab testing.
- Company iterated through "about 50 different types of structures" before finalizing on a **hyperboloid** design — a structural form built from straight elements (first invented by the Ukrainians for a lighthouse tower; also used today for power-station cooling towers and water towers), chosen because straight elements simplify manufacturing and allow a wider range of materials.
- Anchoring approach: reef units are engineered to be anchored initially, then over time thicken with mineral accretion and accumulate marine-life growth, after which their own increased weight helps hold them in place.

### 9. "Seaell" reef in Israel — largest built by the company to date (at time of talk)

## Israel-related content

This is the single Israel-specific project described in the file, from the second ("Seaell") presenter's talk (~01:26:34–01:27:10):

- **Direct quote (paraphrased context, near-verbatim):** "this is really coming back to a picture that Jonathan showed earlier but this is the latest reefs... actually the largest reefs that we've installed to date... with MCC support." (~01:26:34–01:26:46)
- **Structure:** the reef is divided into two broad sections but has three vertical zones / "four rings" — i.e. roughly three tiers going vertically.
- **Material substitution — the key Israel-specific fact:** *"we couldn't get bamboo in Israel. So we've ended up using a willow material, similar to what they put around your garden to protect against the wind."* (~01:26:58–01:27:10) Willow is used in the **top two sections** of the structure.
- **Bottom section — deliberately left open:** left free of skeleton material for two reasons stated explicitly: (1) to give fish a clear area to move in and out of the reef, and (2) scour concern — leaving the near-seafloor zone open lets water move freely forward and backward near the bed, reducing scour effects around the structure.
